rationale: A wins because it keeps the metrics in their lanes. "Duolingo's beta language video chats are holding users for 9 minutes a session" is a clean data hook with the right caveats; B opens with "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high," which turns a DAU record into an engagement claim and creates a fact-checking problem in sentence one. B has some sharper beat labels, but it pads the product-strategy shelf with near-neighbor angles instead of making the founder choose the strongest one.
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo is responding by adding more engagement-driven AI features" overclaims causality; the update does not say these launches are a response to educator criticism.
"Duolingo is doubling down" is lazy posture language and a blacklisted tic; it makes a launch sound like a LinkedIn caption.
"a gamified chess course" is inferred. The facts say the chess course is free for all users, not how gamified that course is.

The markets angle is real, but "for an earnings/markets audience" would be stronger if tied to an actual filing or earnings date; A correctly asks for that proof, but the angle still leans on company-disclosure timing only.
gaps_in_B: "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high" is wrong. The update says daily active users grew to a new high; it does not say engagement hit an all-time high.
"a live public educator critique" invents freshness. The facts say some educators have publicly criticized gamification, not that a live critique is happening now.
"Character.AI-style engagement claims" drags in an outside comparison the update did not supply. That may be a beat context, but here it reads like a borrowed news peg.

"two new product bets in the same quarter" invents quarter framing, and the paywall/free angle plus "free chess course is a bet" angle are close cousins. Pick pricing strategy or category expansion unless Duolingo can prove both.
